expansion:
Myasthenia gravis is correct. The fluctuating ptosis that worsens late in the day and improves with rest is fatigable weakness: the lecture’s sustained-upgaze sequence shows that “the ptosis WORSENS as the position is held” (L30, slide 18). Its myasthenic neuromuscular-junction diagram labels “Receptors blocked by antibody” and “Reduced transmission” (L30, slide 17). The ice-pack finding is especially supportive: after the “Ice Pack Test,” the lecture shows that “BOTH LIDS ARE RAISED” (L30, slide 19). Intermittent binocular diplopia also fits ocular myasthenia, since the lecture shows variable EOM weakness and states that myasthenia can imitate “ANY nerve or muscle palsy” (L30, slide 20).

Multiple sclerosis is wrong because it does not characteristically produce this combination of clearly fatigable ptosis and a marked reversible ice-pack response. It can cause diplopia through central ocular-motor pathway disease, but that is not the pattern demonstrated here (not taken from the course material).

Thyroid eye disease is wrong. The lecture does include double vision from restrictive myopathy, but associates it with lid retraction, proptosis, and discomfort in some positions of gaze (L10, slide 19); its lid signs are explicitly retraction and lid lag (L10, slide 17). These findings differ from fluctuating, fatigable ptosis that improves after an ice pack.

Horner syndrome is wrong. Although it can cause ptosis, the taught associated signs are “Miosis,” “Dilation Lag,” “Apparent enophthalmos,” “Anhydrosis,” and congenital heterochromia (L22, slide 11). It does not account for fluctuating diplopia, fatigability, or the positive ice-pack response (not taken from the course material).
objective: Recognize fluctuating fatigable ptosis with diplopia and improvement after an ice-pack test as ocular myasthenia gravis.
